content_html:
Images as Participating Presences

Agency, Essence, and Spirit across Traditions

Some traditions (e.g., in anthropology of art or indigenous cosmologies) hold that images participate in the life of their subjects—they’re not inert but carry essence, spirit, or agency.

Across many cultures and theoretical frameworks, images are not treated as inert signs. They are participating presences: loci where personhood, spirit, or agency can be present and effective. This sheet synthesizes perspectives from anthropology, indigenous cosmologies, religious image theory, and modern aesthetics.

From Objects to Agents

Alfred Gell reframed artworks as social agents and “indexes” that mediate relations. Agency is distributed across persons and things; an image can compel, bind, protect, or intimidate in concrete social networks.

Presence, Spirit, Relation

  • Aboriginal Australian art: paintings instantiate and reactivate the ancestral Dreaming; images are alive in ongoing ritual and storytelling.
  • African masking: a mask becomes the ancestor/spirit when danced, effecting protection, judgment, or celebration.
  • Amazonian/Andean (e.g., Shipibo-Conibo): kené designs are vessels of cosmological knowledge and healing; patterns hold presence and memory.

Likeness, Presence, Veneration

Hans Belting traces how, before “art” as a secular category, images were primarily presences. In Christian traditions of icons and relics, efficacy derives from participation in the prototype; veneration addresses the person through the image.

Beyond Nature/Culture Splits

Descola and Viveiros de Castro describe ontologies where personhood and agency extend beyond human bodies. Images readily function as nodes where such personhood appears. Latour’s Actor‑Network Theory likewise treats objects as participants in networks of action.

Modern Aesthetics & Lived Practice

Even within modernity, viewers often treat images as alive: speaking to photographs in mourning; attributing power to political icons; or experiencing a sense of presence in portraits. Barthes and Berger help articulate how this “aliveness” is co‑created in viewing.
